issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may use its statutory supervisory jurisdiction to correct a decision that is not according to law, but that jurisdiction is wider than ordinary jurisdictional-error review and narrower than appellate jurisdiction.
material_facts: The dispute arose in proceedings under a rent-control statute, and the reviewing court considered a lower court's eviction decision.
The lower court treated the tenancy as monthly despite a lease deed showing a fixed one-year term.
The reviewing court set aside the lower court's decision after construing the lease deed.
issues.conclusion: The reviewing court acted within its jurisdiction in setting aside the lower court's decision because that decision was not according to law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 35(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 permits the High Court to call for the record of a case under the Act to satisfy itself that the decision is according to law and to make an appropriate order. Under Hari Shankar v. Rao Girdhari Lal Chowdhury, drawing on Bell & Co. Ltd. v. Waman Hemraj, this power is wider than the power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but is not appellate jurisdiction; it is directed to the overall legality of the decision and does not permit intervention merely because the reviewing court might have reached a different conclusion.

predicates.rent_control_supervisory_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding under a rent-control scheme in which a reviewing court examines a lower court's decision.
predicates.lower_decision_not_according_to_law: The lower court's decision rests on a legal error that makes the decision, considered as a whole, not according to law.

issues.definition: When a reviewing court examines a decision in a rent-control proceeding and the lower decision is not according to law, the reviewing court may set it aside.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant whose fixed-term lease has expired by efflux of time is not entitled to a notice terminating the tenancy under the general property-transfer notice provision before eviction proceedings are brought.
material_facts: The lease deed admitted by the tenant provided for a fixed term of one year.
That fixed term had expired before the eviction suit was filed.
The question of notice depended on the term of the tenancy, which was established by construing the lease deed.
issues.conclusion: Because the lease had expired by efflux of time, no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 was necessary.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the fixed-term lease and efflux-of-time principle in concluding that the tenancy had ended according to its stated term. It therefore did not need to decide the broader contention about whether the rent-control statute required a statutory notice before an eviction suit, or whether the notice given complied with section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

predicates.eviction_suit: The proceeding seeks recovery of possession from a tenant.
predicates.fixed_term_lease_expired_by_efflux: The lease fixed a definite term and that term ended before the eviction proceeding was brought.

issues.definition: In an eviction suit, where the fixed lease term has already ended, a termination notice under the general property-transfer rule is not required.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant is liable to eviction for subletting premises without the landlord's written consent when, after an earlier subtenancy ends, the tenant independently inducts new subtenants after the relevant statutory restriction has commenced.
material_facts: After entering into the lease, the tenant sublet some rooms without obtaining the landlord's written consent.
Earlier subtenants had occupied those portions, but their subtenancies ended before the new subtenants were inducted.
The new subtenants were inducted by the tenant and did not hold under the earlier subtenants.
issues.conclusion: The new sublettings without the landlord's written consent attracted the statutory ground for eviction, and the tenant could not claim the Act's protection against eviction on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(b)(i) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 makes a tenant liable to eviction if, after commencement of the Act and without the landlord's written consent, the tenant sublets, assigns, or otherwise parts with possession of all or part of the premises. The existence of earlier subtenants does not prevent the provision from applying where the tenant independently inducts new subtenants after the earlier subtenancies have ended.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks a tenant's eviction under a rent-control scheme that restricts unauthorized subletting.
predicates.tenant_inducted_new_subtenants_after_ear: The tenant independently placed new subtenants in premises after the earlier subtenancies of those portions had ended.
predicates.tenant_lacked_landlord_written_consent: The tenant did not obtain the landlord's written consent to the new subletting.
predicates.induction_occurred_after_restriction_com: The tenant inducted the new subtenants after the restriction on unauthorized subletting had commenced.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, a tenant who independently inducts new subtenants after earlier subtenancies end, without the landlord's written consent and after the restriction has commenced, is not protected from eviction for unauthorized subletting.
